It is proper to observe, that, almost in all cases, whoever makes himself master of an opening with his doubled rooks, must have the advantage: it is of consequence then to the adversary never to give up these kinds of passes.">(h)</span></span></div><div class="move"><span class="move-no">16.</span><span class="ply"><span class="side">White.</span> The king&#x27;s knight&#x27;s pawn, two moves.</span><span class="ply"><span class="side">Black.</span> The same.-</span></div><div class="move"><span class="move-no">17.</span><span class="ply"><span class="side">White.</span> The king&#x27;srook, at its bishop&#x27;s second square.</span><span class="ply"><span class="side">Black.</span> The queen, at her second square.</span></div><div class="move"><span class="move-no">18.</span><span class="ply"><span class="side">White.</span> The queen&#x27;s rook, at its king&#x27;s bishop&#x27;s square.</span><span class="ply"><span class="side">Black.</span> The king, at his knight&#x27;s second square. <span class="note-ref" tabindex="0" data-note="In this situation, the white must make it his principal object, to oblige the adversary to push his king&#x27;s pawn one step, so that he may place, at the fourth square of the same king&#x27;s bishop, a knight, sustained by two pawns: this would entirely decide the game in his favour. The black then ought, in opposition, to find the means of doubling the two rooks, and pushing the queen&#x27;s bishop&#x27;s pawn two moves, to put him again in action.">(i)</span> 1731</span></div></div>
<div class="philidor-notes"><h3>Notes with no reference in the text</h3><p class="note-why">The scan lost the mark that called these, so no move points to them.</p><p><span class="note-letter">(a)</span>Though the getting out the pieces before the pawns, must be avoided as much as possible, I think this play absolutely necefsary in the present situation, to keep the advantage of the move. Nevertheless you might, on the same move, push your king&#x27;s bishop&#x27;s pawn two moves. Such a game, though dangerous in itself, is very good against a player to whom some advantage is given.</p><p><span class="note-letter">(b)</span>If, instead of castling, he had played his queen&#x27;s bishop to your king&#x27;s knight&#x27;s fourth square, you must have played your queen to be knight&#x27;s third square, which would have given you the game: but, if he played the same bishop to his king&#x27;s third square, you must have taken him with yours, and played afterwards your queen to his her knight&#x27;s third square.</p></div>
